prompt:
Create a professional 2D comic character development sheet for an original personal mascot called the heyNag moth. Use the attached moth images only as continuity references, and deliberately improve their anatomy and acting. Landscape composition on a plain warm off-white ground: one large full-body hero drawing occupying the left third, then three smaller full-body sequential acting drawings across the remaining two thirds. No words, labels, panels, logos, decorative shapes, gradients, stage glow, or graphic interface. Keep every antenna, wing, hand and foot fully in frame with generous separation. Crisp confident charcoal linework, simple cream body fills, chartreuse wings and antenna tips, restrained flat color; appeal comes from drawing and acting, not texture or lighting.

This is a curious, talkative, warm comic character with dry timing. Give it a soft compact torso that can bend and twist, a large expressive cream head, one off-center crown tuft and two cheek tufts, a clean lower jaw, a small three-lobed neck collar, two separate expressive arms, two feet, and two chartreuse wings hinged behind the shoulders. Remove the original repeated cloudlike scallops around the entire head and wing edges. Arms attach below the collar and are long enough for convincing crossed-arm thinking. Hands have a readable thumb and three grouped rounded fingers at this scale, with no glove cuffs. Use simple solid charcoal eyes that can deform under lids, independent brows, and a highly movable mouth; no permanent smirk or narrowed smug eye. Preserve the longer antenna on the same anatomical side as the reference—the viewer's right in the front view—and the shorter one opposite. The long antenna is a flexible stem ending in a narrow rounded paddle with a slight forward crook, not a plant leaf. Keep the exact same anatomy, colors, proportions and antenna identity in all four drawings.

Preserve a broad warm face, compact body weight, and recognizably folded moth wings: the increased articulation must not become a skinny rubber-hose insect. Keep the crown tuft small and subordinate to the dominant long antenna.

Hero: a natural three-quarter contrapposto with one planted foot, the other angled casually out, head turned toward us, a warmly amused asymmetric grin, one hand mid-explanation, the other resting near the belly. Oppose the shoulder and hip angles. One wing rests folded and the other sits slightly lifted. The long antenna subtly leans toward whatever has caught the character's attention. A clear character silhouette, not a symmetric mascot wave.

Three-beat acting strip, left to right: First, absorbed thinking through simple charcoal glasses: one arm crossed under the opposite elbow, the other hand actually supporting the chin, weight on one leg, free toe raised ready to tap, head dipping into a small grin; a compressed curved silhouette. Second, an idea arrives before composure can keep up: long antenna springs forward first, eyes suddenly open, torso stretches and pitches forward over the planted foot, one elbow opens, one wing involuntarily lifts while the other stays folded; a tall diagonal silhouette. Include one tiny plain warm lightbulb near the lifted wing, no burst of extra symbols. Third, the character has turned outward to share it: feet set wider to catch its balance, torso in an easy counter-twist, one hand gesturing in an eager explanation, chin slightly tucked, an open warm laugh threatening to break a composed grin; one brow lifted, eyes attentive to the viewer; a broad asymmetric silhouette. Keep the glasses through all three beats. Each pose must change the line of action and center of weight, not merely substitute its face or rotate the entire drawing. Preserve believable hand contacts and avoid merged limbs, floating hands, extra fingers, costumes, jewelry, wings used as extra arms, and imitation of an existing character.
status: Acting exploration. User identified cape-like wings as needing revision; not a final master.
openIssue: Restore recognizable moth wing structure and restrained details.
